<p>A 24-year-old African American woman presents with 4 months of progressive fatigue, intermittent fevers, joint pain in her hands and knees, and a facial rash that worsens with sun exposure. Examination reveals an erythematous malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, painless oral ulcers, and synovitis of bilateral metacarpophalangeal joints. Laboratory studies: hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, white blood cells 3,200/μL (lymphocyte 800), platelet count 95,000/μL, serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL (baseline 0.7). Urinalysis shows 3+ protein and red blood cell casts; 24-hour urine protein is 1.8 g. ANA is positive at 1:1280 (homogeneous pattern). Anti-dsDNA is positive at 320 IU/mL. Anti-Smith antibody is positive. C3 is decreased at 52 mg/dL; C4 is decreased at 8 mg/dL. Renal biopsy shows diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis with subendothelial 'wire-loop' deposits. Which of the following antibodies is most specific for the underlying disease and correlates best with disease activity?</p>


      <div class="explanation-content">
        <h3 class="text-lg font-bold text-[#8c1515] mb-2">Concept explanation</h3>
        <p class="mb-4">Picture a security system that decides you, the homeowner, are the intruder. The alarms go off everywhere at once: skin, joints, kidneys, blood vessels, blood cells. This overreactive security system is lupus. Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is the classic multisystem autoimmune disease, where the immune system attacks DNA, RNA, and other parts of the cell nucleus. Since nuclei sit in every cell, the damage shows up all over the body. The typical patient is a woman of childbearing age, with a female-to-male ratio around 9 to 1, and the disease tends to run more severe in Black, Hispanic, and Asian patients. Part of why it hits women so much harder is that some immune genes that were supposed to be inactivated escape X-inactivation and end up double in number, and estrogen also plays a role in the immune response.</p><p class="mb-4">The core problem is loss of tolerance to nuclear antigens. Normally, when a cell dies by apoptosis, macrophages quietly clear away its nuclear contents (DNA, histones, ribonucleoproteins). In lupus that cleanup fails, the debris piles up, and it gets presented to T cells, which then help B cells make antibodies against DNA, histones, Smith antigen, and more. Those antibodies bind their targets and form immune complexes that circulate and lodge in vessel walls, glomeruli, joints, skin, and serous membranes. At the systemic level this is a Type III hypersensitivity disease. The complexes fix complement, which is why C3 and C4 fall together during a flare as they get used up, as they pull in neutrophils that further damage tissue. A few features also arise type II (direct antibody) mechanism, such as the autoimmune hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and leukopenia.</p><p class="mb-4">It is worth naming the two ways antibodies do the damage here, because lupus uses both. In a type III reaction, the antibody and its target stick together into little clumps called immune complexes that drift through the blood and lodge in the body’s filters, the glomerulus, the joint lining, and small vessel walls, where they switch on complement and pull in neutrophils. In a type II reaction the antibody instead lands straight onto a cell, a red cell or a platelet, and flags it for destruction. Most of lupus runs on the type III route, with a type II sideline that explains the low blood counts.</p><p class="mb-4"><strong>Hypersensitivity Reactions (Types I–IV) </strong></p><table class="w-full text-sm text-left border-collapse border border-slate-300 mb-4"><thead><tr><th class="p-2 bg-[#1b365d] text-white border border-slate-400"><p><strong>Type</strong></p></th><th class="p-2 bg-[#1b365d] text-white border border-slate-400"><p><strong>Mechanism</strong></p></th><th class="p-2 bg-[#1b365d] text-white border border-slate-400"><p><strong>Onset</strong></p></th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td class="p-2 border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-800"><p><strong>I — Immediate (atopic / anaphylactic)</strong></p></td><td class="p-2 border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-800"><p>IgE on mast cells &amp; basophils → degranulation (histamine, leukotrienes)</p></td><td class="p-2 border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-800"><p>Minutes</p></td></tr><tr><td class="p-2 border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-800"><p><strong>II — Antibody-mediated (cytotoxic / receptor)</strong></p></td><td class="p-2 border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-800"><p>IgG/IgM vs a cell-surface or matrix antigen → complement + ADCC + opsonization, OR receptor stimulation/blockade</p></td><td class="p-2 border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-800"><p>Hours</p></td></tr><tr><td class="p-2 border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-800"><p><strong>III — Immune-complex</strong></p></td><td class="p-2 border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-800"><p>Antigen–antibody complexes deposit in tissue → complement → neutrophil damage</p></td><td class="p-2 border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-800"><p>Hours–weeks</p></td></tr><tr><td class="p-2 border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-800"><p><strong>IV — Delayed (T-cell)</strong></p></td><td class="p-2 border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-800"><p>CD4 Th1 cytokines → macrophage / granuloma + CD8 direct cytotoxicity (no antibody)</p></td><td class="p-2 border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-800"><p>48–72 h</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p class="mb-4">Mnemonic: I = Allergic, II = antiBody, III = immune Complex, IV = Delayed</p><p class="mb-4"><img src="data:image/png;base64,"></p><p class="mb-4"><em>Figure 1: EULAR/ACR criteria for diagnosis of lupus</em></p><p class="mb-4">The clinical presentation is ambiguous, hence the comprehensive diagnostic criteria checklist. The skin shows the photosensitive malar (butterfly) rash that spares the nasolabial folds, discoid lesions, and painless oral ulcers. The joints give a non-erosive arthritis. The serosal surfaces inflame into pleuritis and pericarditis. The kidney is the prognostic linchpin, since lupus nephritis drives much of the long-term outcome. The blood shows cytopenias, the nervous system can produce seizures or psychosis, and lupus overlaps with antiphospholipid syndrome, which adds clotting and pregnancy loss. Another form of lupus, drug-induced lupus is the milder, kidney-sparing, anti-histone-positive cousin that resolves when the offending drug is stopped.</p><p class="mb-4">Diagnosis often pairs the clinical picture with serology. A positive ANA at a titer of 1:80 or higher is the entry criterion in the 2019 EULAR/ACR scheme. ANA is very sensitive, since more than 95% of lupus patients have it, but it is not specific, so it also turns up in scleroderma, Sjogren, mixed connective tissue disease, drug-induced lupus, autoimmune hepatitis, and even in some healthy older people. The antibodies that confirm lupus are the specific ones: anti-dsDNA (specific, and its level tracks disease activity, especially nephritis), anti-Smith (the most specific, though it does not track activity), anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB (sicca symptoms and neonatal lupus with congenital heart block), anti-histone (drug-induced lupus), and the antiphospholipid antibodies. </p><p class="mb-4">Treatment uses several drugs alone or together. Hydroxychloroquine is given to nearly everyone because it cuts flares, lowers mortality, and is safe in pregnancy; corticosteroids cover moderate-to-severe disease; and mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, or rituximab are added for organ-threatening problems like lupus nephritis, with belimumab and anifrolumab as newer add-ons. Sun protection matters, since UV light sets off flares by driving keratinocyte apoptosis and exposing nuclear antigens. This patient's wire-loop deposits and diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis are Class IV lupus nephritis, the most aggressive renal pattern, and need prompt, aggressive immunosuppression to head off kidney failure.</p><div class="mt-8 text-xs text-slate-500 italic"><p><em>References: Tsokos, G. C. (2011). Systemic lupus erythematosus. (2019). 2019 European League Against Rheumatism/American College of Rheumatology classification criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus. Arthritis &amp; Rheumatology, 71(9), 1400–1412. https://doi.org/10.1002/art.40930</em></p></div>
